🍁The Sunday Spotlight🍁

The Month in Migraine
A quiet month for the medicines this family uses, with a few things worth knowing. An AI wrote this section.
1. Our own October. Seven migraines logged from Sept. 27 through Oct. 31: Garret four (Oct. 6, 23, 27 and 29), Mom two (Oct. 9 and 29), Dad one (Oct. 6). Twice, two of us logged on the same day: Garret and Dad on Oct. 6, Garret and Mom on Oct. 29. What it means: Garret's four came in two clusters, which fits what his own log has shown before: attacks tend to bunch together. Keep logging; the pattern only shows with the count.
2. Migraine and endometriosis travel together. A Mayo Clinic analysis of 35 studies covering about 13 million women, presented Oct. 20 to the American Neurological Association, found women with endometriosis (womb-lining tissue growing outside the womb) had about 2.3 times the odds of migraine. What it means: it's a link, not proof that one causes the other, but anyone with both kinds of pain should mention both to a doctor.
3. A new kind of rescue pill reaches the last round. TriGemX Bio started phase 3 trials, the final round of testing before an FDA application, for elismetrep, a pill that blocks TRPM8, a "cold-sensing" switch on the nerves of the face and head. What it means: nothing for this winter; first results are expected in mid-2027.
4. A small reassurance on the heart. A Swiss clinic followed 17 people with a past stroke, mini-stroke or heart disease who took CGRP-blocking migraine drugs for up to five years: no new strokes or heart problems, and 13 of the 17 cut their migraine days at least in half. What it means: encouraging, but 17 people with no comparison group is a very small study; call it modest.
Coming down the road. Lundbeck's bocunebart, which blocks a second migraine messenger called PACAP, has a late-stage update expected by year's end, and September's updated prevention guideline from neurologists and headache doctors names no single first-choice drug, leaving the pick to doctor and patient. And the clocks: standard time returned at 2 a.m. today; daylight saving time shifts an hour of daylight from morning to evening from March to early November, CBS explains. Any schedule change can nudge sleep, so the next few nights are worth guarding.

✶The National Wire✶

1

Update: Out of Oleshky

Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky crossed into Ukrainian-held territory Saturday after traveling by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, CBS reports. The roughly 2,000 people left in the city were offered the choice of going to either side; the ceasefire runs through this evening.

2

Trump's Suit Against the Journal Tossed

A federal judge in Miami threw out President Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over its story on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein, saying he was "grasping at straws," NPR reports. The dismissal is with prejudice, meaning the suit can't be refiled.

3

Valkyries Win in Their Second Year

The Golden State Valkyries won their first WNBA title Saturday, beating the Atlanta Dream 68–63 in Game 7, CBS reports. Gabby Williams scored 30 to cap a season that broke WNBA records for viewing and attendance.

☑The Ballot☑

Two Days Out; Last Day to Vote Early
Governor. Kathy Hochul leads Bruce Blakeman by about 13 points. The two newest polls agree: Siena (Oct 19–22) has her ahead 54 to 40 and Marist (Oct 22–25) 53 to 42. What it means: Hochul is a clear favorite going into Tuesday.
NY-26, North Tonawanda. Democrat Tim Kennedy, the incumbent, against Republican Dennis Hannon. The Cook Political Report rates it solidly Democratic.
NY-23, Orchard Park, Dunkirk and Fredonia. Republican Langworthy, the incumbent, against Democrat Gies.
NY-25, Scottsville. Democrat Morelle, the incumbent, against Republican McIntyre.
Down the ballot in North Tonawanda. State Senate: Ortt (R, inc.) against Arida (D). Assembly: Conrad (D, inc.) against Faisal (R); in the open seat, Wydysh (R) against McMurray (D). The city votes yes or no on an $18 million community center at the Keller Building, paid for by a special property tax of about 84 cents per $1,000 of assessed value before grants.
The legislature elsewhere. Orchard Park: Assembly, Burke (D, inc.) vs Dickson (R); Gallivan (R) unopposed for State Senate. Scottsville: State Senate, Helming (R, inc.) vs Mills (D); Assembly, Hawley (R, inc.) vs Wolcott (D). Dunkirk and Fredonia: State Senate, Borrello (R, inc.) vs Guite-Williams (D); Assembly, Molitor (R, inc.) vs Carle (D).
Where to vote early, today only, 9 to 5. North Tonawanda: Wheatfield Community Center or Wendelville Fire Co. Orchard Park: the Community Activity Center on California Road. Scottsville: Henrietta Library, Gates Presbyterian or any of 15 Monroe County sites. Dunkirk and Fredonia: the County Fairgrounds 4-H Building.
The national read. Democrats are favored to take the House; Cook expects them to gain 12 to 25 seats. The Senate is close, tilting Democratic: Democrats lead narrowly in Maine, Ohio and Texas and comfortably in North Carolina, Iowa and Alaska are dead heats, and Kansas has tipped to the Democrat. The president's approval is about 21 points underwater in the average. If the Senate comes down to Maine or Alaska, the tracker notes, control may not be known until mid-November.
Election Day Nov 3, 6 a.m.–9 p.m. · sites and every race: benthambulletin.github.io/election

⛪The Home Wire⛪

1

Rochester · Off to States

The Pride of Rochester Marching Band got a send-off Saturday at Thurgood Marshall Middle School before heading to Syracuse for the 54th New York State Field Band Conference Championship, Rochester First reports. Students, families and neighbors lined up to see them off.

2

Fredonia · Boil Order Lifted

Fredonia's boil-water order is over for all village water customers, including those in Pomfret, after two straight days of clean tests, the county health department says, WIVB reports. The order to conserve water stays in effect.

3

Niagara Falls · Lit in Teal Monday

Niagara Falls, Buffalo City Hall and the Peace Bridge will glow teal Monday night for Alzheimer's awareness, the Niagara Gazette reports. They join more than 1,750 sites worldwide in the Alzheimer's Foundation of America's annual light-up.

★The Marquee★

1

David S. Pumpkins Returns

Tom Hanks brought back David S. Pumpkins to open Saturday Night Live's Halloween show, until James Austin Johnson's Trump interrupted to fret about Tuesday's midterms, Deadline reports. SNL also aired a clip of Patrick Stewart's 1994 episode in tribute.

2

Heidi Klum, Severed Hand

Heidi Klum arrived at her 25th annual Halloween party in New York dressed as a giant, bloody copy of her own left hand, rings and manicure included, CBS reports. Helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits walked her in.

3

Lizzo as Jolene

Lizzo paid tribute to Dolly Parton with a Halloween look copied from the artwork for "Jolene," yellow jumpsuit and platinum wig, Billboard reports. She lip-synced Parton's "Dumb Blonde" in the video.

Last week: what's the best Halloween costume you ever wore?
Gregg: the man from Mercury, an old motorcycle helmet fitted with the dashboard and backup lights from a Mercury, run off a motorcycle battery and wrapped in black, which made him six inches taller. It took first place at Mickey Rats in Jamestown.
